  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }

    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.

    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }

  initializeReadingPreferences();

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">The Statistical Signature of LLMs</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ortal Hadad

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models generate text through probabilistic sampling from high-dimensional distributions, yet how this process reshapes the structural statistical organization of language remains incompletely characterized. Here we show that lossless compression provides a simple, model-agnostic measure of statistical regularity that differentiates generative regimes directly from surface text.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We analyze compression behavior across three progressively more complex information ecosystems: controlled human–LLM continuations, generative mediation of a knowledge infrastructure (Wikipedia vs. Grokipedia), and fully synthetic social interaction environments (Moltbook vs. Reddit). Across settings, compression reveals a persistent structural signature of probabilistic generation. In controlled and mediated contexts, LLM-produced language exhibits higher structural regularity and compressibility than human-written text, consistent with a concentration of output within highly recurrent statistical patterns. However, this signature shows scale dependence: in fragmented interaction environments the separation attenuates, suggesting a fundamental limit to surface-level distinguishability at small scales.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">This compressibility-based separation emerges consistently across models, tasks, and domains and can be observed directly from surface text without relying on model internals or semantic evaluation. Overall, our findings introduce a simple and robust framework for quantifying how generative systems reshape textual production, offering a structural perspective on the evolving complexity of communication.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_classification"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_classification">keywords</h6>large language models, stochastic generation, lossless compression, synthetic text, information dynamics
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rapid diffusion of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping how language is produced, accessed, and circulated <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burton et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Generative systems are now embedded in search engines, productivity tools, knowledge platforms, educational settings, and social media, increasingly mediating everyday interactions with information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wessel et al. (2025)</a></cite>. As a result, large volumes of online text are partially or entirely generated by probabilistic models, often without clear signaling or stable boundaries between human and synthetic content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dugan et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2025)</a></cite>. This shift constitutes not only a technical challenge, but a structural transformation of information ecosystems, with implications for accountability, governance, and epistemic literacy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bender et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Quattrociocchi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At the surface level, LLM outputs often appear coherent and stylistically similar to human writing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Crothers et al. (2023)</a></cite>. This resemblance has fueled, on the one hand, inflated claims about near-human linguistic competence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duncan (2024)</a></cite>, and on the other, a large literature on detection, labeling, provenance, and watermarking of synthetic text <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weber-Wulff and others, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perkins et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchell et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchenbauer et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Empirical evidence, however, shows that detection remains fragile in open-world settings, with performance degrading under domain shift, paraphrasing, translation, post-editing, and changes in model families <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weber-Wulff and others, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perkins et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This brittleness suggests that the central issue is not classifier accuracy per se, but limited understanding of the structural statistical properties that differentiate language produced under distinct generative regimes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Human language arises from complex cognitive and social processes, shaped by intention, communicative goals, pragmatic constraints, contextual grounding, and uneven information exposure across individuals and communities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pinker (2013)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ellis (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Di Marco et al. (2024)</a></cite>. LLM-generated text, by contrast, is produced through iterative sampling from conditional probability distributions learned from large corpora of prior language use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Holtzman et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Even when outputs appear similar, the underlying generative mechanisms differ fundamentally. Recent work has highlighted this divergence from multiple angles. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loru et al. (2025)</a></cite> show that LLMs can replicate human-like judgment outputs while relying on qualitatively different evaluative strategies, leading to surface alignment that masks deeper epistemic mismatches. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Quattrociocchi et al. (2025)</a></cite> formalize these mismatches as epistemological fault lines and introduce the notion of <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Epistemia</em>, in which linguistic plausibility substitutes for epistemic evaluation. Complementarily, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nudo et al. (2025)</a></cite> document <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generative exaggeration</em>, whereby probabilistic generation amplifies statistical regularities in simulated discourse, producing reduced variability relative to human language.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Information-theoretic concepts provide a useful theoretical reference for comparing generative regimes in a model-agnostic setting. Here, in particular, we adopt an approach based on lossless compression. Compression exploits redundancies in symbol sequences, yielding shorter encodings for text that exhibits stronger structural regularity. This connection is classical in information theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cover and Thomas, 2006</a>)</cite> and underlies universal compression schemes such as Lempel–Ziv <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ziv and Lempel, 1977</a>)</cite>. We use <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gzip</span>, standardized in RFC 1952 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deutsch, 1996</a>)</cite>, which operates directly on surface strings without access to model internals, semantic representations, or task-specific features, making it suitable for cross-domain comparisons in partially observable settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We apply this compression-based framework across three contexts of increasing realism: (i) controlled corpora where humans and LLMs produce text under comparable conditions; (ii) generative mediation of a large-scale knowledge infrastructure (Wikipedia vs. Grokipedia); and (iii) fully synthetic social interaction environments (Moltbook vs. Reddit). Compression reveals systematic differences in structural regularity between human and probabilistically generated language, as well as highlighting scale-dependent effects. Rather than proposing a detector of synthetic text or assessing semantic quality, we identify a structural signature of probabilistic language generation with implications across diverse settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>State of the Art</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rapid diffusion of large language models (LLMs) has generated a large and growing literature on distinguishing human-authored text from machine-generated content, largely framed as a detection problem motivated by concerns over misinformation, academic integrity, and content moderation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and others (2023)</a></cite>. Approaches span supervised classifiers, zero-shot statistical methods, watermarking schemes, and analyses of robustness and evasion.
Supervised detection methods typically rely on discriminative models trained on labeled corpora to separate human and machine-generated text. While effective in controlled, in-domain settings, their performance often degrades under domain shift, changes in source models, and simple transformations such as paraphrasing or post-editing. Benchmark datasets such as HC3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo and others (2023)</a></cite> and its extensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. (2023)</a></cite> have been introduced to support evaluation across multiple domains and tasks, including settings where semantic invariance makes detection substantially harder.
Parallel work has explored zero-shot signals derived from language-model likelihoods, token ranks, and related statistics. These methods exploit the tendency of common decoding strategies to concentrate probability mass on high-likelihood continuations, leaving detectable statistical traces. GLTR visualizes token-rank distributions and aggregates simple statistics across sampling regimes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gehrmann et al. (2019)</a></cite>, while related approaches use perplexity, entropy-adjacent measures, and variability indicators such as burstiness, trading simplicity and model-agnosticism for sensitivity to decoding parameters and post-processing.
More recent methods introduce theoretically grounded zero-shot criteria based on properties of the probability landscape. DetectGPT estimates local curvature of the log-probability function via stochastic perturbations, showing that machine-generated text tends to occupy regions of negative curvature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchell et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Fast-DetectGPT improves efficiency by replacing explicit perturbations with curvature proxies derived from conditional probabilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bao et al. (2024)</a></cite>, with further work examining robustness to perturbation strategies and token-level choices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and others (2024)</a></cite>.
An alternative line of work frames detection as a comparison between generative distributions rather than as a classification task. Binoculars contrasts likelihoods assigned by closely related language models, demonstrating accurate zero-shot detection without task-specific training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hans et al. (2024)</a></cite>. This perspective emphasizes structural differences between generative processes rather than purely discriminative cues.
Beyond post-hoc detection, watermarking and provenance methods aim to embed detectable signals at generation time. Kirchenbauer et al. propose a watermarking scheme based on biased token sampling over a secret vocabulary subset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchenbauer et al. (2023)</a></cite>. While effective under cooperative settings, such approaches raise concerns regarding robustness, adversarial removal, and applicability to pre-existing content.
Across empirical evaluations, a recurring finding is the limited robustness of both supervised and zero-shot detectors in real-world conditions, with substantial false positives and false negatives and vulnerability to simple obfuscation strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weber-Wulff and others (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perkins et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Consistent with these limitations, OpenAI discontinued its own AI text classifier due to insufficient accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI (2023)</a></cite>.
Alongside detection-focused approaches, a smaller literature explores lightweight methods based on structural statistical features that avoid large models at inference time. Compression-based classification techniques exploit the link between statistical regularity and compressibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loru et al. (2026)</a></cite>. Berchtold et al. introduce a GZIP-KNN method combining lossless compression with nearest-neighbor classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Berchtold et al. (2024)</a></cite>, connecting to earlier work linking compression and linguistic structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mahoney (1999)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Our work builds on this perspective by using compression not as a detector, but as a signal of statistical regularity, by examining its behavior across controlled corpora, generative mediation of knowledge infrastructures, and fully synthetic social interaction environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Token distributions and controlled statistical regimes</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine how compression responds to statistical token regularity, we generate token sequences with varying levels of Shannon entropy.
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> be a vocabulary and</p>
</div>

<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{1}_{\{t_{i}=w\}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{1}_{\{t_{i}=w\}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the indicator function.

<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To control the statistical concentration in an empirical token distribution, we consider a parametric family of distributions with fixed entropy indexed by a parameter <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in\left[\frac{1}{n},1\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in\left[\frac{1}{n},1\right]</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>

<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The entropy of this distribution is:</p>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">and it is bounded at the extremes:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=1</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{(1)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{(1)}</annotation></semantics></math> is a Dirac distribution and <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\big(p^{(1)}\big)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\big(p^{(1)}\big)=0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\frac{1}{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\frac{1}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{(1/n)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{(1/n)}</annotation></semantics></math> is uniform over <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\big(p^{(1/n)}\big)=\log n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\big(p^{(1/n)}\big)=\log n</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Varying <math id="S3.SS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> therefore defines a continuum of reference regimes ranging from highly uniform to strongly concentrated token distributions. These regimes provide an interpretable baseline for the empirical analyses presented in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, where compression behavior is evaluated across different levels of distributional concentration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Compression-based structural regularity</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From an information-theoretic perspective, lossless compression can be interpreted as an operational probe of effective statistical regularity. Universal coding schemes such as Lempel–Ziv adapt to recurring patterns in symbol sequences without requiring access to the underlying generative process. Therefore, we use it as a model-agnostic measure of structural organization that can be applied consistently across heterogeneous text sources.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each document <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute a compression-based measure using lossless compression. All texts are encoded in UTF-8 and processed as raw byte sequences without tokenization or normalization, ensuring that the analysis depends only on observable surface structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We use the <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gzip</span> algorithm with default settings. Given a document <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, its compressed size <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(x)</annotation></semantics></math> (in bytes) defines the compression ratio</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(x)=\frac{C(x)}{|x|}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(x)=\frac{C(x)}{|x|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|x|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|x|</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the uncompressed size in bytes. Lower values of <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(x)</annotation></semantics></math> indicate higher compressibility and stronger sequential regularity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To examine how structural organization accumulates with length, we compute prefix-based compression curves. For a byte sequence <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=(b_{1},\dots,b_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=(b_{1},\dots,b_{n})</annotation></semantics></math>, prefixes <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x_{1:k}=(b_{1},\dots,b_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1:k}=(b_{1},\dots,b_{k})</annotation></semantics></math> are constructed for increasing <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="R(x_{1:k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(x_{1:k})</annotation></semantics></math> is evaluated independently. This procedure captures how regularity emerges as longer-range dependencies become available to the compressor.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Alongside compression metrics, we compute a limited set of descriptive statistics, including normalized diversity measures and repetition-distance indicators, used solely to contextualize structural differences. These quantities are not interpreted as direct estimates of entropy, nor as proxies for semantic quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">All analyses are applied identically across human-written and machine-generated texts, without relying on model internals, likelihood scores, or semantic representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Datasets</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze three datasets comparing human-written and machine-generated language across progressively more realistic settings:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Controlled Human–LLM Corpus.</span>
We use the publicly available Human-AI Parallel English Corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reinhart et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
For a set of human-written prompts (“Chunk 1”), the dataset provides both human continuations (“Chunk 2”) and model-generated completions produced by six systems: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.1 70B, and their Instruct variants.
This setting enables direct comparison of human and LLM outputs under matched semantic and stylistic constraints.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generative Mediation of Knowledge: Wikipedia vs. Grokipedia.</span>
To study generative mediation within a knowledge infrastructure, we compare 9,279 Wikipedia pages with corresponding Grokipedia entries, where content is rewritten and expanded by a generative system <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hadad et al. (2026)</a></cite>.
Pages are selected based on high reference counts and revision activity to focus on entries with substantial rewriting.
Analyses are conducted at the page level, with prefix-based measurements computed at the sentence level.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fully Synthetic Social Interaction: Moltbook vs. Reddit.</span>
We compare Reddit discussions with Moltbook, a platform populated by autonomous LLM agents generating posts and threaded comments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>.
Reddit data are restricted to pre-2018 posts to minimize the presence of AI-generated content.
Moltbook data were collected between January 31 and February 10, 2026<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                    <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                    
                    
                    
                  https://moltbook-observatory.sushant.info.np/export</span></span></span>, and Reddit data were obtained via the Pushshift API <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baumgartner et al. (2020)</a></cite>.
For each platform, we sample 10,000 posts stratified by length into four categories: <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">low</span>, <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">mid</span>, <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">high</span>, and <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">very high</span>, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Di Marco et al. (2024)</a></cite>. This stratified sampling preserves variability in textual length despite the highly skewed distribution of social media content toward short posts. The analyses reported here focus on the central <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">mid</span> and <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">high</span> length categories, resulting in a final dataset of 20,000 posts for each platform. To ensure comparability across platforms, identical preprocessing steps are applied, including removal of non-textual elements (e.g., URLs, emojis, markup) and normalization of whitespace and encoding.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this first section, we introduce the intuition behind using compression as a tool to detect LLM-generated texts.
Our primary goal is to establish an interpretable baseline linking token distributional concentration to compression behavior. To empirically investigate this connection, we rely on the methodology described in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Token distributions and controlled statistical regimes ‣ 3 Methods ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>. In brief, we consider a parametric family of probability distributions (Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Token distributions and controlled statistical regimes ‣ 3 Methods ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>)) whose entropy is controlled by a parameter <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>. We then generate <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> equally spaced values of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> in the interval <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[\frac{1}{n},1\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[\frac{1}{n},1\right]</annotation></semantics></math> and generate synthetic texts from the corresponding distributions. For each generated text, we compute the compression ratio (Eq. (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.2 Compression-based structural regularity ‣ 3 Methods ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>)) at different entropy levels. Additional implementation details are provided in the Methods section.
The results of this analysis are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(A), where we observe a positive relationship between these two quantities: higher vocabulary entropy is associated with higher compression ratios, that is, lower compressibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given this result, it is of interest to locate the entropy and compression values obtained by human-written and LLM-generated texts. We do that by considering the Human-AI Parallel English Corpus dataset. Because the compressibility of text is dependent on its length, we first ensure that only human and LLM documents of comparable length are considered. Indeed, as presented in the inset of Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(A), the distributions of words for human and LLM documents in the dataset are considerably different. The former peaks at 479 words, while the latter shows much higher heterogeneity. For this reason, we restrict our analysis to documents between 466 and 489 words, which correspond, respectively, to the first and third quartiles of the distribution for human texts. However, all results are consistent when considering the full dataset.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18152v1/fig1.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/452;" width="452" height="452"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(A)<span id="S4.F1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Relationship between vocabulary entropy and compression ratio for texts generated from word distributions with fixed entropy. The colored points show the average values for Humans and LLMs. The bars indicate one standard deviation from the mean. The inset displays the density distribution of document length (number of words) for human-written and LLM-generated texts. </span>(B)<span id="S4.F1.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Compression ratios distribution for human-written texts, LLM-generated texts, and randomly generated texts. Higher compression ratios correspond to lower compressibility. Each group contains <math id="S4.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> documents. </span>(C)<span id="S4.F1.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Average compression ratio of human-written and LLM-generated texts according to the number of sentences in the text. The shaded area shows the interquartile range of the distribution of compressions. For LLM-generated text, as the length increases, compressibility also increases, unlike human text.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The colored points and bars in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(A) locate human and LLMs in terms of average entropy and compression.
While entropy values are broadly comparable across the two groups, more substantial differences emerge in their compression ratios: on average, human-written texts achieve higher compression ratios than LLM-generated ones.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This pattern is further highlighted in panel B, which displays the distribution of compression ratios in a balanced sample including 1000 documents for each group.
The distributions reveal that LLM-generated texts display lower median compression ratios compared to human-written texts. At the same time, they exhibit a higher heterogeneity, particularly in the left tail of the distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For reference, we also include a benchmark based on randomly generated documents, each constructed by sampling 479 words, i.e., the mode of the human document length distribution, from the full vocabulary of the dataset, using both uniform and weighted strategies, generating <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> documents for each.
In the first setting, words are selected uniformly at random from the vocabulary. In the second, they are sampled according to the empirical word distribution estimated from the joint corpus of human and LLM texts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">As expected, these random sequences exhibit substantially lower compressibility than both human- and LLM-generated texts, with uniform sampling yielding the highest ratio values. Their near-uniform word usage leads to high entropy and minimal exploitable structure, making them inherently less compressible.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, Panel C reports the differences in compression ratios between human- and LLM-generated texts as document length increases. For each document, we compute the compression ratio incrementally: first considering only the first sentence, then the first two sentences, and so on. We then compute the average and IQR of these distributions, grouping by the number of sentences. As shown in the figure, after roughly 20 sentences an increasingly high textual regularity and redundancy are reflected in the compression ratio curve for LLMs. In contrast, for humans, the metric stabilizes, indicating that human-generated documents do not exhibit increasing regularity as the number of sentences grows; instead, compressibility remains constant throughout the entire text.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Discriminative Strength of Compression Features</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on the compression differences observed above, we examine additional measures that quantify the statistical regularity of the sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conditional compression.</span> This metric approximates the incremental compression cost of the second half of a document given the first, providing a proxy for context-dependent predictability. It is computed by taking the difference <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(x+y)-C(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(x+y)-C(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and normalizing it by the length in bytes of <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., dividing by <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|y|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|y|</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average and slope of prefix compression curves.</span> For each document, we measure the compression ratio as more characters are progressively included. Then, we compute the average over the range, and estimate its linear slope, which characterizes the average compressibility of prefixes and the rate at which structural regularity stabilizes as the sequence grows.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Word-order contribution metrics.</span> To assess the specific contribution of word order to compressibility, we generated a shuffled version of each document by randomly permuting words within sentence boundaries. We then compare the original and shuffled texts using two measures: (i) the compression ratio gap, defined as <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(x_{\text{shuffled}})-R(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>shuffled</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(x_{\text{shuffled}})-R(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, and (ii) the Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2004)</a></cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Normalized character and word entropy.</span> Complementing compression-based measures, we compute normalized entropy at the character and word levels to measure how evenly they are distributed in the text.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Type-Token Ratio (TTR).</span> We compute the type-token ratio, the proportion of unique words in a text, as a standard measure of lexical diversity and vocabulary richness.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Repetition distance features.</span> For each word, we compute the average and standard deviation of the number of words separating consecutive occurrences. This quantifies the frequency and regularity of repetitions, reflecting structural redundancy.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18152v1/feature_distributions.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:367/555;" width="367" height="555"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution of structural and compression-based features across human-written and LLM-generated texts in the Human–AI Parallel Corpus.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1.1 Discriminative Strength of Compression Features ‣ 4.1 Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we show the distribution of these metrics across human and LLM-generated text from the Human-AI Parallel Corpus. This comparison reveals notable differences, even between different model families. GPT models, in particular, display higher conditional compression, lower prefix variability, and sharply peaked distributional profiles, indicating that their sequences stabilize quickly and remain strongly constrained by prior context. Although GPT outputs show comparatively high lexical diversity, they remain more compressible overall, implying that redundancy arises from structural regularity rather than simple word repetition. Llama 3 models occupy an intermediate regime between GPT and human text, while instruction tuning increases variability and shifts distributions closer to the human baseline without eliminating the separation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To further evaluate the discriminative power of the proposed compression-based features, we trained a Histogram-based Gradient Boosting Classification Tree <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> using only the features described above.
We consider three classification settings of increasing granularity. In the most fine-grained setting, we train a seven-class classifier to distinguish between Human, GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Llama 3 70B, Llama 3 70B Instruct, Llama 3 8B, and Llama 3 8B Instruct. The classifier achieves an overall accuracy of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.65" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.65</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.65</annotation></semantics></math> (macro F1 = <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.65" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.65</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.65</annotation></semantics></math>). GPT-family models and human text are identified more reliably (F1 scores between <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.75</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.75</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.82" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.82</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.82</annotation></semantics></math>), while base Llama models are more frequently confused (F1 scores between <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.46" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.46</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.46</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.66" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.66</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.66</annotation></semantics></math>). Notably, this performance is comparable to prior detection work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reinhart et al. (2025)</a></cite> reporting <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="66\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>66</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">66\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy using 60 lexical, grammatical, and rhetorical features. This suggests that metrics related to statistical regularity can already capture much of the separable signal.
When collapsing labels into Human, GPT, and Llama, accuracy rises to <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.93</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.93</annotation></semantics></math> (macro F1 = <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.90" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.90</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.90</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating that compression features strongly encode family-level generative signatures. Finally, for the binary Human vs. LLM task, the classifier achieves <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.93</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.93</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy (macro F1 = <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math>). LLM outputs are detected with very high precision and recall (F1 = <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.96</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.96</annotation></semantics></math>), while human texts remain the more challenging class (F1 = <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.80</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For model explainability, we perform SHAP analysis on the binary classifier, with the aim of quantifying the impact of each feature on pushing a prediction toward either class. The results, in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 Discriminative Strength of Compression Features ‣ 4.1 Controlled Human vs LLM Corpus ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, reveal that compression-based features and lexical-statistical measures contribute most strongly to the model’s decision boundary.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18152v1/global_feature_importance.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/248;" width="333" height="248"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Global feature importance based on mean absolute Shapley values for the Gradient Boosting Classifier. Bars indicate the average magnitude of each feature’s contribution to the predicted probability of the Human class across the test set.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Generative Mediation of Knowledge: Wikipedia vs Grokipedia</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the previous section established compression as a proof of concept under controlled generation, here we examine its behavior in a setting where human-authored content is rewritten and expanded by LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Wikipedia and Grokipedia provide parallel versions of the same encyclopedic content, with Grokipedia consisting of LLM-mediated rewritings of original Wikipedia pages. This setting allows us to examine how compression behaves when human-curated knowledge is partially reshaped through probabilistic generation, and whether such mediation introduces measurable structural differences in the resulting text.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Consistent with the approach used for the Human–AI Parallel Corpus and described in Methods, we start by computing the compression ratio through an incremental prefix analysis, where documents are decomposed into sentences and progressively extended one sentence at a time. Prefix values are aggregated into 20 uniformly spaced bins (minimum 100 observations) and summarized by mean and interquartile range.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Generative Mediation of Knowledge: Wikipedia vs Grokipedia ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (A) shows that differences in compression ratios begin to emerge after a certain number of sentences.
Around 50 sentences, the interquartile ranges of the two distributions show a diminishing overlap, suggesting that statistical regularities accumulate as text length increases and recurrent structures become more exploitable by compression. As the prefix length approaches 500 sentences, the observed gap progressively narrows. Beyond a certain threshold, this reduction can in part be attributed to the way Grok operates. In particular, Wikipedia pages are predominantly rewritten by Grok in the initial part of the page <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Triedman and Mantzarlis (2025)</a></cite>. This portion is also the most frequently accessed by users <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lamprecht et al. (2021)</a></cite>, which likely incentivizes more intensive revisions at the beginning of the document. As the prefix extends to include text portions where LLM intervention is comparatively limited, the proportion of human-written text increases and the difference between human and LLM-generated text gradually disappears.
Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Generative Mediation of Knowledge: Wikipedia vs Grokipedia ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (B) reports the distribution of four relevant metrics. Conditional compression is slightly lower for Grokipedia, indicating reduced incremental compression cost in LLM-mediated text. At the same time, normalized word-level entropy is higher, suggesting broader lexical dispersion. In contrast, Wikipedia texts exhibit more frequent word repetition with lower variance. These patterns differ from those observed in the controlled completion setting, likely reflecting both the longer document structure and different prompting conditions underlying generative mediation. Rewriting human-generated text with LLMs, particularly within an encyclopedic setting, may therefore alter lexical statistics while preserving a lower overall compression rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Employing the same model specification and features used for the Human–AI Parallel Corpus, on this dataset, we obtain a binary classification accuracy of <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.85</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.85</annotation></semantics></math> (macro F1 = <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.85</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.85</annotation></semantics></math>). Wikipedia articles are identified with high recall (<math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.94" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.94</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.94</annotation></semantics></math>; F1 = <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.86" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.86</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.86</annotation></semantics></math>), while Grokipedia pages reach F1 = <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.84</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.84</annotation></semantics></math>, with higher precision (<math id="S4.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.93</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.93</annotation></semantics></math>) but lower recall (<math id="S4.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.76</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.76</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18152v1/wiki_grok_combined_figure.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/172;" width="476" height="172"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(A)<span id="S4.F4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Average compression ratio of Wikipedia and Grokipedia page texts as a function of the number of sentences in the text. The shaded area represents the interquartile range of the compression ratio distribution. </span>(B)<span id="S4.F4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Distribution of Conditional Compression Ratio, Normalized Word-Level Entropy, Mean Repetition Distance, and Repetition Distance Variability across texts from Wikipedia and Grokipedia pages.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Fully Synthetic Social Interaction: Moltbook vs Reddit</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend the analysis to a fully synthetic social setting, comparing human-generated discussions on Reddit with agent-driven interactions on Moltbook, where all content is produced by LLM-based agents. This scenario allows us to examine how compression behaves when conversational dynamics themselves are generated probabilistically rather than emerging from human interaction. Specifically, here we employ the individual post as the unit of analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Compression ratios are computed following the same procedure described in the Methods and used for the other two datasets. Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Fully Synthetic Social Interaction: Moltbook vs Reddit ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>(A) reports the average compression ratio as a function of the number of sentences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to the two settings analyzed above, differences between Moltbook and Reddit persist only over a limited range of post lengths, and the gap between the two narrows after approximately 25 sentences. Further, over the shorter range of post lengths considered here, LLM-generated content shows a slightly larger compression ratio, corresponding to lower regularity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure  <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Fully Synthetic Social Interaction: Moltbook vs Reddit ‣ 4 Results ‣ The Statistical Signature of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>(B) shows that Moltbook interactions exhibit higher lexical diversity, reflected in a rightward shift in unique word ratio, while maintaining comparable overall compressibility. In contrast, Reddit displays higher normalized compression distance and slightly stronger conditional compression, indicating greater sensitivity to sequential ordering and local predictability. The prefix ratio trend remains largely similar across corpora, suggesting comparable incremental redundancy dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These results suggest that fully synthetic interaction environments do not simply amplify the structural signatures observed in previous sections. Instead, the emergence of compression-based differences appears to also depend on the scale and structure of the generated text. Since the texts in this case are short and fragmented, we cannot observe the structural regularity that tends to emerge as the length of a text increases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we should also consider the role of the prompting conditions underlying Moltbook generation. Prompts aimed toward conversational text generation may encourage LLMs to adopt a more casual, context-local, and human-like discourse style that deviates from their baseline generation. We hypothesize that such conditioning attenuates the emergence of systematic long-range regularities that become detectable in extended informational texts, and alters stylistic features in such a way that generated messages effectively show lower regularity and thus compressibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To complement the analysis presented above, we apply the same model specification and feature set used for the previous sections. On this task, we obtain a binary classification accuracy of <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math> (macro F1 = <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math>). Performance is highly balanced across classes: Reddit posts are identified with precision and recall <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math> (F1 = <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math>), while Moltbook posts achieve precision <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math> and recall <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.87" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.87</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.87</annotation></semantics></math> (F1 = <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18152v1/reddit_moltbook_combined_figure.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/171;" width="476" height="171"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(A)<span id="S4.F5.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Average compression ratio of Moltbook and Reddit comments as a function of the number of sentences in the text. <section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we examine whether lossless compression can serve as an operational proxy for identifying structural statistical differences between human language and text produced or mediated by large language models. We show that compression-based analysis offers a simple and interpretable way to study how generative systems reshape linguistic structure across tasks and environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across three progressively more complex settings, i.e., controlled continuation tasks, generative mediation of encyclopedic knowledge, and fully synthetic social interaction, we observe that compression consistently captures differences in structural organization between human and LLM-generated language. In controlled continuation tasks, we find that compression reveals a clear separation between human- and LLM-generated text, particularly as a greater number of sentences are included in the analysis. This indicates that probabilistic generation concentrates sequences into more regular and redundant patterns. In generative mediation of encyclopedic content, compression reveals how rewriting reorganizes structure while lexical dispersion increases, highlighting a decoupling between vocabulary diversity and sequential regularity.
In fully synthetic conversational environments, however, compression-based separation is only observed over a short range of text lengths. Short conversational units and this particular generative regime may limit the accumulation of long-range statistical dependencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our findings indicate that compression captures a structural footprint of plausibility-driven language production. Importantly, this effect should not be interpreted as an evaluation of semantic quality or truthfulness. Compression reflects differences in the generative process rather than differences in meaning. Further, the observed patterns suggest that statistical regularization emerges gradually as generated text becomes longer and more structurally cohesive, rather than appearing uniformly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As synthetic content becomes increasingly embedded within information ecosystems, understanding these structural shifts is essential for characterizing the dynamics of large-scale language production. Future work may explore how compression-derived signals interact with human post-editing, alternative decoding strategies, and hybrid human–machine production pipelines, as well as their implications for the governance of synthetic information environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
